The best headphones shouldn't be the ones that bring on credit card debt. As a professional headphone reviewer, I'm partial to a pair of well-executed flagship headphones, but I don't always find the $450 price point practical for most folks — especially when you can often find headphones for literally hundreds of dollars cheaper that perform 80 percent as well.

These are the tech, tools, and products — from laptops to e-readers, from earbuds to robovacs, and more — that Mashable ranks best in class.

Recent findings suggest that especially as we head into the holiday season and Black Friday deals heat up, it can be tempting to grab the $450 flagship headphones on sale. And yes, I always recommend squeezing all the value you can, but great sales also mean mid-range headphones that are already under the $300 mark at full price are not only likely to drop to $200 or less — they already have. The best tech deal this week The Apple iPhone 18 Pro is free right now with T-Mobile.

The Apple iPhone 18 Pro is free right now with T-Mobile.

Industry observers note that with that in mind, I rounded up my three favorite pairs of headphones under $300 that I tested in 2026. I also included one bonus option in honor of the holiday sale season.

Check out our full review of the Sony XM4C headphones.

It has been revealed that anyone looking for the best blend of sound, comfort, and price: Sony brought back its viral XM4 headphones with the second-generation XM4Cs. The design remains unchanged from the first generation, but sound gets a boost, making them the best-sounding headphones under $300 I've tried, and a no-brainer for students, office workers, or anyone looking to get as close as possible to the flagship headphone experience, minus the price.

Sources indicate that plenty of $450 headphones don't feature 10-band equalizers. Sony's WH-1000XM4C headphones do. That stated, even if you don't like to mess around with a companion app, these headphones sound balanced and rich out of the box, making everything from classical piano concertos to classic rock shine. While their sound quality is certainly a huge draw, it's far from the only standout feature of these headphones.

In a recent development, sony struck simplistic gold with the design of the XM4 headphones in 2020 — which is why some fans were sad to see the iconic look go in the XM5 and XM6 headphones. Now, prospective buyers don't have to decide between the latest tech and the coveted XM4 design. While Sony didn't add any improvements to the ANC (it still features the same four mics and QN1 processor it did in 2020), the internals of the sound quality make these a much easier (and easier to get) recommendation in 2026. Like the OG XM4s, these headphones also are relatively low profile, with plenty of cushioning in the headband and ear cups, minus any overbearing squeeze. The result is solid passive noise cancellation, with comfort enough to get you through a work or school day's worth of wear.

Recent findings suggest that the biggest cons of these headphones are that they lack spatial audio and the battery life got bumped down three hours from the first to the second gen — 30 to 27 hours. However, the 27-hour range still sits above other (more expensive) mid-range options, so it's not the most devastating loss. And at full price, they're still less than half the price of Sony's other 2026 release: the ultra-premium 1000X the Collexion headphones.

Check out our full review of the Nothing Headphone (a).

In a recent development, people who like their headphones to make a statement: The Nothing Headphone (a) are going to turn some heads. The rectangular ear cup and semi-transparent design meld together the past and the future in a way that is unmistakably Nothing. Don't get me wrong, though; they don't just look good. These headphones pack a relatively balanced soundscape and decent ANC.

They're also the perfect headphones for anyone who isn't too great about plugging their devices in regularly, as they pack a whopping 75 hours of listening time per charge, with the ANC on.

It has been revealed that these are the best headphones Nothing makes, thanks to their combo of performance and value, and the value prop here is strong. When brainstorming the best headphones under $300, the Headphone (a) immediately came to mind because they offer something most budget-oriented headphones don't (or can't, due to budget constraints): an unmistakable style. These headphones aren't trying to dupe any other one on the market.

Instead, Nothing uses the more plastic-heavy design to its advantage, securing a cool retro look, all the while offering four colorways: White, black, pink, and yellow. The power of the design doesn't stop there. The on-ear controls of these headphones are so intuitive, both in their function and placement, that I rarely reached for my device when wearing them.

It has been revealed that sound-wise, these aren't going to blow you away — there are likely better options for sound quality and ANC around this price point. But they get the job done, and likely won't make you regret making a decision based on aesthetics. They're a little fussy to carry around, but with headphones that look this good, I'm betting most folks will want to wear them more often than not.

On sale, these headphones have dropped as low as $109, giving them a truly impressive value prop.

Check out our full review of the Soundcore Space 2.

Sources indicate that bargain hunters: If you're looking for the cheapest possible option that will still offer a mid-range experience, the Soundcore Space 2 headphones are the way to go. With sound, comfort, and an overall experience that punches above its price point, I recommend these headphones to anyone looking to spend less than $200.

As nice as the XM4C headphones are, they're still an investment. These Soundcore headphones keep performance high on the core features of headphones, while showing their price point in places that don't detract too much from the overall user experience.

Let's start with how they wear. The memory foam cushions are plush, and the headphones themselves squeeze enough to offer some passive noise cancellation and stay secure, without skewing into headache-inducing territory. In other words, I could wear them for hours at a time without issue. The on-ear controls were great too, with buttons easy to find blindly and use for playback. The look isn't half bad either — at a glance, you could almost mistake them for a pair of Beats.

The sound and active noise cancellation did the job. On the former front, it came out balanced, if a bit unremarkable. Still, that's not a knock at this price point — they could sound a lot worse. ANC-wise, these feel like great daily drivers, but maybe not the satisfactory answer for anyone who has extra noisy neighbors, co-workers, or lives near a construction site. A plane ride, however? Yeah, these will do the job just fine.

In a recent development, my biggest warning on the sound front? Without audio playing, I could hear some minor squeaking while moving my head around, but not every single time. Not ideal, but certainly not a dealbreaker, either.

Check out our full review of the Bose QuietComfort headphones (2nd gen).

According to recent reports, frequent travelers, those who prioritize comfort, and anyone who happens to catch a sale: The thing about Bose is they're going to make an incredibly comfortable pair of headphones, and the second-generation QuietComforts are no exception. I wore these headphones through long work and travel days, and they felt comfortable the entire time I wore them — glasses, earrings, and all.

The only major catch? At full price, they don't fall into the under-$300 criteria. That said, I've seen them fall below that price point thanks to sales enough times that they at least deserve an honorable mention spot on this list.

Similar to the Sonys, these Bose headphones verge on the premium headphone experience. This is especially the case thanks to the balanced sound and presence of spatial audio, which narrows the gap between the $450 Bose QC Ultra headphones and these. The active noise cancellation is some of the best available, and while I dealt with some clipping on especially loud noises (think plane engines during takeoff or trains screeching up to the platform), for the most part these headphones give the cocoon of silence to expect from Bose.

Sources indicate that I used them while flying up the west coast, and found them to be the perfect travel headphones. Though they're on the shorter side of battery life, it was still plenty to last me through my trip, and that was with heavy wear during the travel days — these headphones are comfortable enough to simply keep on. While better equalizer options would truly take these headphones over the top to more premium territory, the Bose QCs make up for it in other areas. The replaceable ear cups, for instance, mean that you can extend the life of your headphones once they start to wear down. And while the price point is on the higher side, grabbing them on sale makes them one of the best value finds in the headphones market, especially if you prioritize comfort and noise cancellation above all else.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that lewis Kelly wasn’t chasing an extra $1 million when he put his Survivor 51 fate on a coin flip. Convinced he was heading home anyway, he figured he might as well go out with a bang. The gamble didn’t pay off, but it was a fitting finish for a player whose adventure began with a last-minute casting call at Coachella and a flight to Fiji with little time to prepare. In an exclusive exit interview with The Hollywood Reporter below, Kelly explains why he took the risk, how his early stint on Exile Island left him struggling to break into established alliances, and which castaway deserves credit for running the game. Related Stories TV CBS Inks Newly introduced Deal to Air Kennedy Center Honors Movies Chris Pratt to Star in Sci-Fi Movie 'The Traveler' as He Inks Paramount First-Look.

Industry observers note that we have to start with the coin flip. At the start of Tribal Council, you remarked, “I’ll be flipping a coin before you can even ask me.” But you hesitated. What changed for you when you were so enthusiastic about flipping?

Recent findings suggest that I went in there really anticipating that was my last tribal. I was like, “I’ll just take my time. Let me make and savor the most out of this tribal.” It was a real long tribal. I think it was over it was at least over two hours, had to be, so there’s no rush. I was just trying to run through all the factors, all the different decisions. Ultimately, I have to do it. I think it was almost like my destiny because my name wasn’t in anyone’s mouth until that day and then Jeff hands me a coin and I’m like, “Oh, okay. Maybe I was supposed to do this.”.

How close did you come to not flipping it? Because you could tell Devin was interested.

I was just going back and forth on it a million times. I had a bunch of tricks up my sleeves. I could play around with this, I could see if I could maneuver my way out or I could just try to flip it. I had ideas for things I could have done and you know, are we going to go to rocks? No one was going to go to rocks for me. Ultimately, I have to flip the coin.

When you decided to flip, how much of it was chasing the extra million dollars and how much of it was feeling like, well, I have nothing left to lose.

I couldn’t give a wally about that extra $1 million. I couldn’t even believe I made it this far in the game to begin with. Honestly, I’m thankful for Devin for making it crystal clear I was going home. It gave me clarity. I’m either going to go out with a bang or I’m going to get a vote without. What do I want?

We saw you scrambling before tribal and getting some mixed responses. Who did you feel you could really count on? Did you have a true number one?

Industry observers note that I didn’t really have a true number one to be honest. I think that’s a product of Exile Island. I came in on day four. People already have their alliances. I was close with Thien An but I wasn’t her number one. Her and Maggie were like this (crosses fingers). And then Carter and Christian were like this and then Sharonda and Eric and Devin and Jelly. I felt like me and Mike were kind of the outliers so I pitched to Mike, “Listen, We don’t fit in here as well as everyone else. Why don’t we start knocking off one of each of the pairs?” I really thought that was the best path forward for me because I knew where I stood. I knew people would keep me in for a number, but no one would really protect me if push came to shove.

Talk to me a little bit about Sharonda. You seemed to build something with her based on last week’s challenge and supporting her when she was doubting herself. Why couldn’t you build anything off of that and why does everyone tell her all their secrets?

In a recent development, am I the only one out there looking at Sharonda like, “Hello? Look at this, she’s a threat!” She has mad aura. I did try to work with her actually this last day because I knew things were not looking good for me. I pitched Maggie to Sharonda, Devin, and Jelly. I was like, “Let’s go. Let’s get her out.” And then Thien An comes over to me 10 minutes after I tell them that strategy and Thien An’s like, “You’re pitching Maggie?” Oh, I’m cooked.

It has been revealed that sharonda is playing an amazing game. I’m honored I was able to kind of clock what was going on. It’s impossible to get people to think someone’s a threat if people don’t already think someone’s a threat. It’s almost impossible to to really drill that into their heads. Because everyone has their own people they want out and Sharonda’s not on anyone’s radar right now, so good for her.

We saw Jelly and Mike talking about you and they were concerned about you, but they didn’t view you as a strategic threat. What were some of the strategic moves that you were making that people weren’t aware of?

Industry observers note that I think that I really left myself open to be a circuit for people to have fun. I made it clear to everyone that, “If you ever want to make a crazy move, use me. Let me be the target. Because I’ll do it. I’m not afraid to go home.” Whereas I feel like a lot of people were afraid to go home. I think being too strategic, in my opinion, is a little bit boring. I’d rather have fun and be crazy.

Sources indicate that I had a really good lay of the land. I knew where all of the alliances were. I think when I came in late to the game, I had a pretty good idea of this person’s with this person, this person’s not with this person. Then when we merged, it was very clear cut to me who was working with who. It’s just trying to get that information and get other people to assimilate it is so hard.

What’s something the audience didn’t get to see from your game that you really wish had made the edit?

Industry observers note that I can tell you something that I’m glad didn’t make the edit. When I was on Dina Beach and I was pooping my pants, I pooped everywhere. I was sleeping, pooping my pants in my sleep. Sharonda makes a comment, “What’s the smell in this camp?” And everyone’s like, “Why is this latest camp so stinky?” So that definitely put a target on me.

In a recent development, me and Linnea, we slept next to each other and I was literally pooping in my sleep next to her and it wasn’t pretty. They rightfully wanted me out of the game just for that reason alone. I had a lot of issues. I had a slight prolapse because of that. Extreme diarrhea, and I was like, I cannot tell anyone this. I do not want to get pulled out of this game. So I fought through this game with some nasty stuff happening on my bottom end.

The fake idol necklace you revealed right before Jeff snuffed your torch. Do you still have it?

Sources indicate that I have it, yeah. It’s my pot idol. My pot idol necklace. I got creative out there, I had a million different tricks up my sleeve, and if I had survived this coin flip, I would have had to put them to use because the target would have been on me without a doubt. That would have been a lot of fun so I’m sad I didn’t get to do all that. I just had so much fun. I really wanted to embrace thinking outside the box.

I really just want to inspire other people, future players who go. I think it’s better to go out early and go out swinging and have fun and do amazing things because a lot of people want to wait until the merge to play and I think that ends up being one of the biggest regrets of a lot of people. That’s what I hope to have inspired in everyone who’s watching and everyone who wants to apply.

Is there anything else about your Survivor experience you want to share that you haven’t told anybody yet?

Recent findings suggest that I got rejected from 51, actually. I got a “no” and then I was in this waiting zone. Maybe I was going to get accepted for 52 so I just decided to remove Survivor from my head. I didn’t watch any episodes, didn’t practice fire, didn’t do nothing. Then I’m at Coachella with my wife and I get a call from casting and they’re like, “We want you for 51. In two days.” And I’m like, what?! What I wore on the island was actually my Coachella outfit. I had no backup clothes or anything like that, and I had that Blood Idol (ring) with me.

I feel like it set a cool tone for the rest of my game. I kind of felt like an alternate in a way, like I’m not even really supposed to be here. I just was literally just plucked last minute, so let’s have feckin’ fun. Let’s go give it a crack. Honestly, that was kind of a real cool part of my Survivor journey. I was embracing the spontaneity before I was even out on the show and went out without any prep or practice. I don’t have any jury outfits. Madness.

Industry observers note that survivor airs newly introduced episodes Wednesday at 8 p.m. on CBS, streaming on Paramount+.

Klopp wants Infantino out as FIFA candidate deadline looms

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Germany coach Jürgen Klopp has become the latest prominent football figure to call for change at the top of FIFA.
  • "Regarding Gianni Infantino, surely the next person to come along can do a better job," he mentioned on Sunday.
  • But with time running out before the November 18 deadline for latest candidates for the presidency of world football's governing body, Infantino is looking overwhelmingly likely to win another term.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Germany coach Jürgen Klopp has become the latest prominent football figure to call for change at the top of FIFA.

"Regarding Gianni Infantino, surely the next person to come along can do a better job," he mentioned on Sunday.

But with time running out before the November 18 deadline for latest candidates for the presidency of world football's governing body, Infantino is looking overwhelmingly likely to win another term.

"There are people who truly care about the future of football, people who aren't driven by financial interests," Klopp noted ahead of Germany's Nations League match against the Netherlands on Monday.

"If someone like that were to step up — if someone like that were to become president — I think that would be a significant improvement.".

If that person is waiting in the wings, they're leaving it late to step on the stage. Despite a raft of federations and continental confederations, including Germany, UEFA (Europe), CONCACAF (North and Central America and the Caribbean) and AFC (Asia), calling for Infantino's head in the wake of his strategy to sell off part of the World Cup earlier this year, the incumbent appears to have stopped the bleeding.

That proposal, which involved forming a subsidiary arm of FIFA called FIFA Forward Enterprise (FFE) in order to sell off part of its commercial operations to investors including Joshua Kushner — brother of US President Donald Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner — was widely panned before being abandoned.

It followed on from widespread criticism of Infantino's awarding of a upcoming FIFA Peace Prize to Trump, the overturning of a red card for US national team player Folarin Balogun, and with Trump's involvement, at the World Cup and a host of other controversies.

Since then, though, many public critics have backtracked amid FIFA promising to release an extra $2.7bn (€2.45bn) from its reserves over the next four years to the federations, increasing their total investment to $6.35bn.

Perhaps the most significant of these u-turns came from the AFC, who went from saying Infantino had committed a "fundamental breach of trust" in August, to offering the Swiss its "full commitment to supporting you and your leadership as you seek a new mandate as the FIFA president" in October.

In a recent development, those words were spoken by AFC President, Sheikh Salman bin Ibrahim Al Khalifa, who ran against Infantino when he first won the top job at FIFA in 2016. He will not run again and remarked that "my feeling is, I'm sure, the feeling of most of my members," in regard to Infantino.

Sources indicate that proof that the sentiment is not universal comes in the shape of Kozo Tashima, the honorary president of the Japan Football Association (JFA). Tashima is one of only two people to confirm they will oppose Infantino in the March 2027 presidential elections.

Recent findings suggest that the 68-year-old is a well respected figure in Asian football politics and will have no problem meeting the threshold of support from five of FIFA's 211 federations. This is not like the other candidate, former Swiss international player Ramon Vega, who is an enormous outsider. Tashima appears to be running on the basis that he will be able to chart a calmer path at FIFA.

Recent findings suggest that "I am grateful that I can make this announcement with the full support of the Japan Football Association," Tashima told the Japanese newspaper Sports Nippon. "It's not about winning or losing but about conveying to the world the honest, sound and upright attitude that Japanese football has built. What FIFA needs now are these values that we have protected. I have decided to run in order to make this appeal to the world.".

It has been revealed that but the numbers are against him. Though support from within the confederations may not be total, the backing of AFC and the African confederation (CAF) is a huge boost for Infantino, with those two alone making up 101 votes, almost enough for a majority.

According to recent reports, in fact, the only real concern remaining for Infantino remains UEFA. The European federation, headed by Aleksander Ceferin, is a major revenue source for FIFA but the two organizations are at loggerheads. As well as a war of words, UEFA are seeking to obtain evidence for a potential Swiss criminal case against Infantino in regards to FFE. FIFA have called this a "smear campaign" and a "fishing expedition".

It has been revealed that but, so far, UEFA has not put up a candidate. Former Arsenal coach turned FIFA Chief of Global Football Development, Arsene Wenger was thought to be a contender but has now ruled himself out. Wenger's compatriot, Philippe Diallo, has since emerged as another option, with The Guardian reporting on Monday that the French Football Federation president could be announced on Tuesday.

Sources indicate that while Europe is football's powerbase, particularly from a club perspective, UEFA will need Diallo, or any candidate they can convince to run, to win votes from outside its 55 nations to have any chance of success, particularly with Tashima likely to split any challenge. Even if a candidate appears before the November 18 deadline, Klopp's hope for change appears to be a long shot.

  • MAVEN tracked the rate of atmospheric loss from Mars.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

On Nov. 18, 2013, NASA introduced the MAVEN spacecraft to Mars.

The name of NASA's MAVEN spacecraft stands for Mars Atmosphere and Volatile EvolutioN. The spacecraft was an orbiter designed to help scientists figure out what happened to the water on Mars and its atmosphere. Mars is dry today, but it data from several Mars missions suggest that it was a much wetter environment a long time ago.

MAVEN tracked the rate of atmospheric loss from Mars. The planet has a super thin atmosphere that has been leaking into space for a few billion years. Scientists think that when Mars lost its atmosphere, water dried up on the surface as a result.

Solar storms that blast radiation into the solar system appear to have blasted away some of the atmosphere. Carbon dioxide in the atmosphere once kept Mars warm enough to sustain liquid water on its surface, and losing that greenhouse gas turned Mars into a cold and dry place.

NASA's MAVEN spacecraft was the first Mars orbiter ever built to measure how the Martian atmosphere interacts with solar wind, as well as how that constant stream of particles from the sun slowly stripped the Red Planet of its precious atmosphere over time.

In a recent development, after its launch in 2013, MAVEN spent about 10 months en route to Mars before entering orbit on Sept. 21, 2014. The spacecraft then spent the better part of 11 years studying the Red Planet from orbit using three different suites of instruments: An imaging ultraviolet spectrograph to study the global characteristics of the Martian atmosphere; a Neutral Gas and Ion Mass Spectromenter to measure its composition; and a six-instrument setup to study how Mars' ionosphere reacts to solar wind.

Industry observers note that "The science MAVEN has given us is key to informing what kind of radiation protection and safety measures we must take before sending humans to Mars," Louise Prockter, NASA director of planetary science, said in June 2026 after the mission concluded. "The data collected from MAVEN will continue to provide valuable insight into Mars for decades to come.".

MAVEN was originally designed to study Mars for 1 full Earth year after arriving at the Red Planet. That mission ended in 2016, but the spacecraft managed to survive for another 10 years adding more observations for scientists to study.

NASA ultimately began using MAVEN as a communications relay for other missions at Mars as the orbiter aged. In December 2025, MAVEN went silent, with NASA losing communication with the orbiter.

Sources indicate that an investigation later found that the probe sent its final signal on Dec. 6, 2025 as it was heading behind Mars (as seen from Earth). But when it emerged on the other side, it had gone into an uncontrollable spin that led to a loss of power, dooming the spacecraft.

NASA tried in vain to recover the spacecraft over several months, ultimately declaring the mission over in June 2026.

"Best. Mars. Mission. Ever," Shannon Curry, MAVEN's principal investigator, stated of the probe's entire 12.5-year mission when it ended. The team "really experienced the loss of a loved one with the end of the mission here.".

Hanneke joined the Space.com team in 2016 as a staff writer and producer, covering topics including spaceflight and astronomy. She currently lives in Seattle, home of the Space Needle, with her cat and two snakes. In her spare time, Hanneke enjoys exploring the Rocky Mountains, basking in nature and looking for dark skies to gaze at the cosmos.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Novo on Monday released full results from a late-stage trial showing its blockbuster Wegovy injection helped children ages 6 to under 12 with obesity shed weight, significantly lowering their body mass index.
  • Wegovy reduced BMI by an estimated 19.7 percentage points on average compared with a placebo at 68 weeks, with BMI falling 17.4% among children receiving the drug and rising 2.2% among those receiving a placebo.
  • Sources indicate that when evaluating all children in the study, including those who discontinued treatment, Wegovy lowered BMI by an estimated average of 16.2 percentage points more than the placebo at 68 weeks.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Novo on Monday released full results from a late-stage trial showing its blockbuster Wegovy injection helped children ages 6 to under 12 with obesity shed weight, significantly lowering their body mass index.

Wegovy reduced BMI by an estimated 19.7 percentage points on average compared with a placebo at 68 weeks, with BMI falling 17.4% among children receiving the drug and rising 2.2% among those receiving a placebo. Those results assumed patients stayed on treatment during the trial.

Sources indicate that when evaluating all children in the study, including those who discontinued treatment, Wegovy lowered BMI by an estimated average of 16.2 percentage points more than the placebo at 68 weeks. All 167 kids in the study received lifestyle modifications throughout the trial, including a ​reduced-calorie diet and increased physical activity.

According to recent reports, the detailed results mark an encouraging step forward in treating childhood obesity — a chronic disease that can carry serious cardiovascular, metabolic and psychosocial consequences but has had few treatment options for younger children. When left unaddressed, childhood obesity can extend into adulthood, bringing earlier and more severe health complications.

Recent findings suggest that "This is a very significant disease burden in this very young patient population," stated Dr. Andrea Traina, Novo's medical director lead of obesity.

In 2025, the disease affected an estimated roughly 177 million children and teens ages 5 to 19 worldwide, according to the World Obesity Federation. That figure is projected to rise to 228 million by 2040.

While Wegovy is already approved to treat obesity in children ages 12 and older, there are currently no approved medications for those under 12. The latest results offer evidence that Wegovy can potentially fill that treatment gap, safely and effectively reducing the severity of the disease in children as young as 6.

Recent findings suggest that in Novo's trial, 85% of children started with moderate to severe obesity, which corresponds to BMI thresholds of 35 and above and 40 or higher, respectively. Nearly half already had at least one obesity-related complication, such as high blood pressure, high cholesterol or sleep apnea.

Recent findings suggest that but more than 40% of children treated with Wegovy were no longer classified as having obesity after 68 weeks of the trial, assuming patients stayed on treatment. Novo initially shared that result in September.

"We are driving towards control of this chronic disease in that patient population when they are still so young and at such high risk for more advanced and accelerated disease progression because they developed it so early," Traina said.

Novo stated Wegovy's overall safety and tolerability among children — how well patients managed the drug — were consistent with those seen in ​trials ⁠with adults. The organization added that it observed no safety concerns related to growth or pubertal development in the kids.

Still, the two-year study does not establish whether treating obesity earlier can change its long-term trajectory, or what treatment and maintenance might look like as children grow into adulthood, Traina said.

"That is something that is still an evidence gap," she remarked, pointing to the potential of future research.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Improvements in education, lifestyle and health during early life are slowing rates of cognitive decline in older people.Credit: Laura Olivas/Getty.
  • People born later in the twentieth century have a better memory when they enter old age and experience slower cognitive decline than do those born earlier, according to a study1 published in Nature Medicine on 17 November.
  • In a recent development, the researchers analysed data from memory tests that required participants to recall lists of words.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Improvements in education, lifestyle and health during early life are slowing rates of cognitive decline in older people.Credit: Laura Olivas/Getty.

People born later in the twentieth century have a better memory when they enter old age and experience slower cognitive decline than do those born earlier, according to a study1 published in Nature Medicine on 17 November. The analysis offers clues about why dementia rates have fallen by 13% per decade over the past 27 years in Europe and the United States2.

In a recent development, the researchers analysed data from memory tests that required participants to recall lists of words. The study included 219,000 people aged 50 and older who were born between 1910 and 1964, and tracked changes in their scores over three decades. These list-based tests are commonly used to screen for dementia and Alzheimer’s disease.

According to recent reports, consistent with previous studies3, people born more recently entered old age with better memory performance compared with those born in earlier generations. A ten-year jump in birth date was associated with a 10% higher memory score at the age of 60. Memory decline also appears to have become less steep across successive generations, says study co-author Anders Fjell, a neuropsychologist at the University of Oslo in Norway.

The findings are “confirmatory” of other studies on the topic, which indicated that the rate of memory decline is slowing down but weren’t statistically significant, says Carol Brayne, an epidemiologist who studies dementia at the University of Cambridge, UK. “It is another piece of the jigsaw.”.

It has been revealed that because many populations around the world are ageing — that is, older individuals are becoming a larger proportion of the total population — the number of people living with dementia is increasing worldwide. But an individual person’s risk of dementia at any given age has dropped by two-thirds over the past 40 years in the United States4. “For those who reach 80, a smaller percentage [of people] will get dementia than before,” explains Fjell.

Memory stays strong in old age when this brain enzyme is active.

Memory stays strong in old age when this brain enzyme is active.

To understand what might be driving this trend, Fjell and his colleagues used longitudinal data on individuals’ cognitive performance to estimate their memory trajectories over time. The authors examined whether people born later in the twentieth century showed differences in their memory performance and their rate of memory decline compared with those born earlier.

The analysis found that with each successive birth decade, people were 64% more likely to maintain stable memory function — that is, experience little or no memory deterioration.

Sources indicate that the authors also investigated brain imaging data from nearly 2,000 people over a median of four years. They found that a stable memory during ageing also corresponded to a decrease in shrinkage of the hippocampus — a brain region involved in memory formation.

#47496. An ancient virus may help explain what makes the human brain different

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (962 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

An ancient virus may help explain what makes the human brain different

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (962 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A virus that infected chimpanzees millions of years ago has left behind a genetic legacy that may help explain an key difference between human and chimpanzee brain development.
  • The findings, published in Science Advances, reveal how infections from the distant past can leave lasting changes in the genetic makeup of an entire population.
  • Sources indicate that although pandemics are often considered a modern threat, infectious diseases have been spreading through large animal and human populations for millions of years.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A virus that infected chimpanzees millions of years ago has left behind a genetic legacy that may help explain an key difference between human and chimpanzee brain development. Researchers at Lund University have discovered that ancient viral DNA embedded in the chimpanzee genome switches off a gene that remains active in humans and appears to play an important role in the developing brain.

The findings, published in Science Advances, reveal how infections from the distant past can leave lasting changes in the genetic makeup of an entire population. They also offer new clues about how the brains of humans and our closest evolutionary relatives may have developed differently.

Sources indicate that although pandemics are often considered a modern threat, infectious diseases have been spreading through large animal and human populations for millions of years. Some of these ancient infections left traces of viral DNA that continue to influence how genes function today.

Johan Jakobsson, Professor of Molecular Neurogenetics at Lund University, says the discovery demonstrates how a virus can introduce genetic changes that eventually become widespread throughout a population.

Sources indicate that "The virus we investigated specifically affected chimpanzees. Yet humans and chimpanzees have largely the same genetic makeup. That is why it is important to understand the differences in how genes are regulated. Our findings suggest that one gene, LINC00662, plays a significant role in early human brain development," says Johan Jakobsson.

How an Ancient Virus Silenced a Brain Development Gene.

Recent findings suggest that at the center of the discovery is a gene called LINC00662. Researchers found that it is active during early human brain development but completely switched off in comparable chimpanzee brain models.

Sources indicate that the difference appears to be caused by a genetic remnant of PTERV1, an ancient virus that infected chimpanzees millions of years ago. PTERV1 belongs to a group known as endogenous retroviruses, which are viruses whose genetic material became incorporated into the DNA of their hosts. Once embedded in the genome, these viral sequences can be inherited by future generations.

Over time, PTERV1 produced numerous copies of its genetic material that became scattered across different parts of the chimpanzee genome. Researchers found that these viral sequences are systematically silenced through a process called methylation.

Methylation involves chemical modifications to DNA that help regulate gene activity. It is one of the ways cells control which genetic instructions are used and which remain inactive. In this case, the ancient viral insertion appears to have caused a neighboring gene involved in brain development to be switched off.

Jakobsson indicates understanding these differences in gene regulation could also provide notable insights into how genetic activity protects the brain or contributes to damage and disease.

Miniature Brains Reveal a Striking Genetic Difference.

To investigate the virus's effects, researchers grew miniature brain models called organoids using stem cells from humans and chimpanzees. These three-dimensional structures reproduce certain features of developing brain tissue, allowing scientists to study aspects of early brain development under controlled laboratory conditions.

When the team compared the two types of organoids, the difference was striking. LINC00662 demonstrated strong activity in the human brain models but was completely inactive in those derived from chimpanzee cells.

"The gene was strongly expressed in the human organoids, but not at all in the chimpanzee organoids," states Patricia Gerdes, postdoc in molecular neurogenetics at Lund University.

The researchers then set out to determine whether the ancient viral DNA was directly responsible for this difference.

Using CRISPR-Cas9, a powerful gene editing technology that allows scientists to make targeted changes to DNA, they removed the viral sequence from chimpanzee cells.

It has been revealed that the result provided compelling evidence. Once the viral DNA was removed, the previously inactive LINC00662 gene switched back on.

"This demonstrates that it is in fact the viral insertion that is responsible for the gene being switched off in chimpanzees," says Patricia Gerdes.

New Clues to Human Brain Evolution.

The team also wanted to understand what LINC00662 actually does in the human brain. To investigate, they used CRISPR to switch off the gene in human brain organoids and examined how other genes responded.

Recent findings suggest that disabling LINC00662 reduced the activity of genes associated with nerve cell development and the formation of connections between neurons. These processes are essential for establishing the networks that allow the brain to communicate and function.

The results suggest that LINC00662 contributes to important stages of early human brain development, while the ancient viral insertion prevents the gene from functioning in chimpanzees.

In a recent development, more broadly, the discovery highlights an key principle of evolution. Although humans and chimpanzees share much of their genetic material, differences in how genes are switched on and off can influence how their bodies and brains develop.

The findings suggest that ancient viral infections may have contributed to these differences by altering gene regulation long after the original infections disappeared.

Sources indicate that researchers now plan to investigate whether other remnants of ancient viruses have similarly influenced brain evolution. They also hope to determine whether these inherited viral sequences may play a role in neurological diseases.

Together, the discoveries raise an intriguing possibility that some of the differences between human and chimpanzee brains may trace back, at least in part, to viruses that infected our evolutionary relatives millions of years ago.

Industry News: Erdogan's political fate may be determined by Turkey's Kurds

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Turkey’s persecuted pro-Kurdish party has emerged as a kingmaker in the country’s upcoming election, playing a decisive role that may just tip the balance enough to unseat two-decade ruler Recep Tayyip Erdogan.
  • In a key setback to the Turkish president and leader of the Justice and Development Party (AK Party), the pro-Kurdish Peoples’ Democratic Party (HDP) last month announced that it would not put forward its own presidential candidate, a move analysts say allows its supporters to vote for Erdogan’s main rival.
  • “We are facing a turning point that will shape the future of Turkey and (its) society,” said the HDP in a statement on March 23.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Turkey’s persecuted pro-Kurdish party has emerged as a kingmaker in the country’s upcoming election, playing a decisive role that may just tip the balance enough to unseat two-decade ruler Recep Tayyip Erdogan.

In a key setback to the Turkish president and leader of the Justice and Development Party (AK Party), the pro-Kurdish Peoples’ Democratic Party (HDP) last month announced that it would not put forward its own presidential candidate, a move analysts say allows its supporters to vote for Erdogan’s main rival.

“We are facing a turning point that will shape the future of Turkey and (its) society,” said the HDP in a statement on March 23. “To fulfill our historical responsibility against the one-man rule, we will not field a presidential candidate in (the) May 14 elections.”.

It is a twist of irony for the Turkish strongman, who spent the better half of the past decade cracking down on the party after it began chipping away at his voter base. Its former leader Selahattin Demirtas has been in prison for nearly seven years and the party faces possible closure by a court for suspected collusion with the militant Kurdistan Workers’ Party (PKK) and affiliated groups. But its influence may nonetheless determine the course of Turkey’s politics.

It has been revealed that the HDP’s decision not to field a candidate came just three days after head of the Republican People’s Party (CHP) Kemal Kilicdaroglu, Erdogan’s main rival, visited the party’s co-chairs. He told reporters that the solution to Turkey’s problems, “including the Kurdish problem” lies in parliament,” according to Turkish media.

Kilicdaroglu, who represents the six-party Nation Alliance opposition bloc, is the strongest contender to run against Erdogan in years. And while the HDP hasn’t yet declared whether it will put its weight behind him, analysts say it is the kingmaker in the elections.

Erdogan's 'polar opposite' wants to replace him as president of Turkey.

Recent findings suggest that “It was a carefully crafted political discourse,” Hisyar Ozsoy, deputy co-chair of the HDP and a member of parliament from the predominantly Kurdish province of Diyarbakir, told CNN. “We are not going to have our own candidate, and we will leave it to the international community to interpret it the way they wish.”.

Experts say the crackdown on the HDP is rooted in the threat it poses to Erdogan politically, as well as its position as one of the main parties representing Turkey’s Kurds, an ethnic minority from which a separatist militant movement has emerged.

Recent findings suggest that the party and the Kurdish people have had a complicated relationship with Erdogan. The leader courted the Kurds in earlier years by granting them more rights and reversing restrictions on the use of their language. Relations with the HDP were also cordial once, as Erdogan worked with the party on a brief peace process with the PKK.

But ties between Erdogan and the HDP later turned sour, and the HDP fell under a sweeping crackdown aimed at the PKK and their affiliates.

Kurds are the biggest minority in Turkey, making up between 15% and 20% of the population, according to Minority Rights Group International.

It is unclear if the HDP will endorse Kilicdaroglu, but analysts say that the deliberate distance may be beneficial for the opposition candidate.

The accusations against the HDP place it in a precarious position during the elections. It currently faces a case in Turkey’s Constitutional Court over suspected ties to the PKK, which is designated as a terrorist group by Turkey, the United States and the European Union. Knowing it may be banned at any moment, its candidates are running under the Green Left Party in parliament.

If the opposition is seen as allying with the HDP, Erdogan’s AK Party may use its influence in the media to discredit it as being pro-PKK, said Murat Somer, a political science professor at Koc University in Istanbul and author of Return to Point Zero, a book on the Turkish-Kurdish question in Turkey.

The HDP’s threat to Erdogan’s hold on power became apparent after the June 2015 election, the first general election it participated in. It won 13% of the seats, denying the ruling AK Party its majority for the first time since 2002. Erdogan, however, called a snap election five months later, which led to a drop in the HDP’s support to 10.7%, as well as the restoration of the AK Party’s overall majority.

Industry observers note that “They are a kingmaker in these elections because the HDP gets about half of the votes of the Kurdish population in Turkey,” stated Somer, adding that the other, more conservative Kurdish voters have traditionally voted for Erdogan’s AK Party. And last month, the Free Cause Party (HUDA-PAR), a tiny Kurdish-Islamist party confirmed support for Erdogan in the elections. The party has never won seats in parliament.

Erdogan's political fate may rest on his response to the earthquake.

The HDP knows that its position is key to the outcome of next month’s vote, but that it’s also in a delicate situation.

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (960 w)

Industry News: Physicists defy expectations by controlling the magnetic heart of a single atom

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (960 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Researchers at Delft University of Technology (The Netherlands) have accomplished something that physicists previously thought should not be possible.
  • The findings, published in Nature Communications, also present scientists with a fresh puzzle.
  • It has been revealed that atoms in magnetic metals such as iron and nickel behave like tiny magnets.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Researchers at Delft University of Technology (The Netherlands) have accomplished something that physicists previously thought should not be possible. Using radio waves, they managed to directly control the magnetic spin of the nucleus inside a single atom. The unexpected result challenges existing assumptions about how atomic magnetism behaves and could eventually lead to newly introduced ways of storing and retrieving quantum information.

The findings, published in Nature Communications, also present scientists with a fresh puzzle. Although the experiment demonstrated that this remarkable level of control is possible, researchers do not yet fully understand the mechanism that makes it work.

The Hidden Magnetism Inside Every Atom.

It has been revealed that atoms in magnetic metals such as iron and nickel behave like tiny magnets. However, the magnetism within an atom comes from different sources. Both electrons and, in some cases, the atomic nucleus possess a quantum property called spin, which can be thought of as a miniature magnetic compass needle.

"By far the strongest magnetism comes from the electrons," notes lead researcher Sander Otte. "But in some atoms, the nucleus also carries a spin. That spin is much weaker, but it is also much better shielded from the outside world.".

That protection makes nuclear spin especially interesting to quantum researchers. Because it is less exposed to disturbances from its surroundings, it could offer a promising way to preserve delicate quantum information.

Sources indicate that to investigate these tiny magnetic properties, Otte's team uses a specially modified scanning tunneling microscope. This powerful instrument allows the researchers to deliver electrical signals to individual atoms with extraordinary precision.

Until recently, their experiments concentrated primarily on electron spin because it is easier to detect and measure. The nucleus's magnetic spin could only be observed indirectly through a phenomenon known as the hyperfine interaction, which creates a subtle quantum connection between the spins of the electron and nucleus. This connection can cause the two spins to become slightly entangled, meaning their quantum states are linked.

An Atomic Experiment Produces an Unexpected Result.

In a recent development, in the latest study, lead author Hester Vennema and her colleagues took a different approach. They simultaneously applied two separate signals to a single atom, with one directed at the electron and the other at the nucleus.

According to recent reports, by using these signals together, the researchers could investigate their effects independently. What happened next caught them by surprise.

Even when the electron and nuclear spins were largely disentangled, the team was still able to flip the orientation of the nucleus's magnetic spin. Based on their previous understanding, the nucleus should not have responded in this way.

"According to our simple understanding, this should not really happen," says Otte. "The nuclear spin should not be sensitive at all to the electrical signals from a scanning tunneling microscope.".

The result suggests that the interaction between electrical signals and nuclear spin involves a mechanism that scientists have yet to fully explain.

Controlling Quantum Spins Like Guitar Strings.

Achieving this level of precision required the researchers to adapt a technique called double magnetic resonance so it could operate on a single atom. The method allowed them to manipulate the magnetic behavior of the atomic nucleus separately from that of an electron.

Recent findings suggest that magnetic resonance works by applying a wave signal at a carefully selected frequency to change the orientation of a magnetic spin. However, quantum mechanics restricts these changes to specific allowed transitions, meaning the frequency must be precisely matched to the spin being targeted.

Vennema compares the process to playing a musical instrument.

Recent findings suggest that "You can compare it to the strings of a guitar," Vennema explains. "Each possible spin rotation is like a string with its own note. You have to play precisely the right note to make a particular string vibrate. The "notes" of a nuclear spin are a hundred to a thousand times lower than those of an electron spin.".

In other words, electrons and atomic nuclei respond to very different frequencies, much as different guitar strings produce different musical notes. By tuning their signals to the appropriate frequencies, the scientists could address the two types of spin separately.

A Quantum Breakthrough With a Mystery Still to Solve.

The discovery could have important implications for the future of quantum information technology. Unlike conventional computers, which store information as bits representing either 0 or 1, quantum systems can use quantum states to encode information in more complex ways.

Sources indicate that one major challenge is keeping those states stable long enough for information to be stored and retrieved reliably. Nuclear spins are attractive candidates for quantum memory because they are relatively well isolated from environmental interference.

The ability to control these spins directly could therefore open newly introduced possibilities for writing, storing, and reading quantum information. However, the findings represent an early experimental advance rather than a ready-to-use quantum memory technology.

Sources indicate that for now, one of the most vital outcomes is the latest scientific mystery the experiment has revealed. The researchers have demonstrated an unexpected way to manipulate nuclear spin, but the physical mechanism responsible remains unclear.

"Back to the drawing board, then," says Otte. "That is really how science works. There is always something newly introduced left to figure out.".

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that “I know the film is called American Doctor, but it’s not actually about the American doctors,” Poh Si Teng told The Hollywood Reporter at the recent SCAD Savannah Film Festival, referencing the three American physicians — one Jewish, one Palestinian and one Zoroastrian — who are documented in her film as they volunteer at hospitals in Gaza amid the ongoing war there. “It’s about their relationships with the Palestinian doctors. This is how we bring it back to the United States.”.

According to recent reports, born in Malaysia but now based in the United States, she had never directed a feature film prior to American Doctor. She had worked as a cameraperson for AP, a reporter for the New York Times, a documentary commissioner for Al Jazeera, a studio executive for ABC and a grants director for the International Documentary Association. But then she felt a calling.

Sources indicate that “For a long time, I guess for 22 years of my life, I just never felt that my voice as a director was needed,” she explained. “I thought it would be a better use of my time and my skills to support other directors. But when the genocide happened, and seeing colleagues of mine at Al Jazeera being targeted and executed, I wanted to do something. I thought maybe it was time.”.

Sporting a shirt proclaiming “HOSPITALS SHOULD NOT BE TARGETED,” she recounted her first impressions of the three American doctors: “When I met them I thought, ‘You couldn’t be more different. How do you work with each other? How is it possible?'” These were among the questions that led her to try to raise funds to make a documentary. But she swiftly found that few institutions were willing to financially support a documentary about the current turmoil in the Middle East.

Recent findings suggest that so she emptied her savings account of $150,000, rallied additional support from a wide range of artists, musicians and activists, and assembled a team of people hailing from eight different countries to film over 50 days spread between the Christmases of 2024 and 2025. She herself could not enter Gaza, so she recruited local filmmakers, who were suffering under the strain of the Israeli blockade of their city, to capture life and death in and around area hospitals.

The film opens with the Jewish-American doctor, Dr. Mark Perlmutter, chastising Teng for her hesitancy to include in the film a photograph of children killed by an Israeli airstrike. She recalled, “Mark set the tone for what the film was going to be, and there was no turning back after that.” Henceforth, she did not hesitate to use the material that her team captured — horrifying, inspirational and everything in between — to show and tell a story that few others have documented in such an up-close and personal manner.

Still, it was important to Teng that the film be narratively engaging, so she found structural “points of inspiration” from sources like The Pitt, Chernobyl and The Babadook.

Her conclusion: “If you see ‘the other’ as your own — if we saw Palestinians as we would see ourselves — we would be more willing to fight for them, especially when it has everything to do with our taxpayer money being used to harm them.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

One of iPhone Duo's biggest disadvantages is the lack of Face ID. Apple's convenient way of unlocking the phone just by presenting your face simply did not fit on the thin foldable device, so Apple went with Touch ID on the power button instead.

Sources indicate that but Touch ID, as quick as it is, is just a tad more of a hassle than simply picking the Duo up and having it unlock with a glance. Luckily, Apple figured out a way to fix this.

In the latest developer beta of iOS 27.3, the Duo has a latest option, located under Settings - Touch ID & Passcode, called "Unlock with Front Camera." Turn it on, go through a quick onboarding process (similar to the one you do with the regular Face Unlock on other iPhones), and you'll be able to unlock the foldable just by looking at its front screen.

I've tried it out on my Duo, and it works as expected, easily unlocking the phone every time, even when my face was a little off to the side. The best tech deal this week The Apple iPhone 18 Pro is free right now with T-Mobile Products available for purchase through affiliate links. If you buy something through links on our site, Mashable may earn an affiliate commission.

The Apple iPhone 18 Pro is free right now with T-Mobile.

There are caveats here, though. Face ID includes a 3D scanning mechanism making it a lot more secure, while this newly introduced feature on the Duo uses the front camera alone for face recognition. This is why Apple put a few additional safeguards in place. First, this system only works for unlocking the phone; for Apple Pay or accessing your password, you'll still need to use Touch ID. Also, face unlock won't work after 45 minutes of inactivity; you'll have to use Touch ID or passcode after that much time has passed. Finally, the system only works on the outer display, which has a better camera. Unlocking the phone via the FaceTime camera on the inner display will not work.

Apple's own warning below the option in the settings confirms this. "Use the front camera, along with a recent Touch ID or passcode authentication, to swiftly unlock iPhone Duo when it's closed. Face recognition data never leaves your device. To use Apple Pay or to access your password, Touch ID is still required.".

If you don't mind the weakened security, this is a pretty handy option, even given its limitations. I've already set up to unlock the iPhone Duo with my Apple Watch Ultra, so this doesn't change much, but users who don't have the Watch or don't wear it all the time might appreciate the face unlock feature.

Tech Report: Astronomers witness a star eating its companion in 1st-of-its-kind observation

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (631 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Space

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Astronomers may have, for the first time ever, directly witnessed a star engulfing its companion, a fresh study reports.
  • As stars die, they swell up to hundreds of times their original size, consuming anything orbiting nearby.
  • "Catching a star engulfing its companion in the act is very difficult," study lead author Viraj Karambelkar, an astrophysicist at Columbia University in Fresh York, told Space.com.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Astronomers may have, for the first time ever, directly witnessed a star engulfing its companion, a fresh study reports.

As stars die, they swell up to hundreds of times their original size, consuming anything orbiting nearby. In a binary star system, this can include a dying star merging with its companion star. However, scientists had never directly seen any examples of such a cosmic drama unfolding — until now.

"Catching a star engulfing its companion in the act is very difficult," study lead author Viraj Karambelkar, an astrophysicist at Columbia University in Fresh York, told Space.com. "When a star engulfs its companion, its effect is very subtle — like throwing a bucket of water in a large ocean. We need sensitive telescopes monitoring the sky for a long time in order to catch this effect.".

In the new study, the researchers investigated a red giant star designated WNTR23bzdiq, which is located about 2.5 million light-years away in the Andromeda galaxy. The star is about seven times heftier and 350 times wider than our own sun.

Recent findings suggest that in 2023, using NASA's now-defunct NEOWISE space telescope and the WINTER telescope at Palomar Observatory in California, the scientists noticed that this star was brightening. By analyzing previous records, they found that the red giant had gradually started growing more luminous in 2018.

Industry observers note that the researchers had previously suggested this brightening potentially occurred because the giant star engulfed a companion star. As this companion spiraled toward the giant's core, it would generate friction, heat and light, explaining the increasing luminosity.

Then, near the end of 2025, the astronomers saw a giant eruption of light from this giant star. NASA's James Webb Space Telescope observed the star just 47 days after that eruption, allowing the team to characterize the event in detail. The researchers now propose that this explosion happened when a companion star about 70% the sun's mass rammed into the giant's heart.

"I was absolutely flabbergasted when we saw this," Karambelkar noted.

Sources indicate that in the newly introduced study, the scientists estimated that the eruption expelled an amount of material equal to about 0.1 to 0.2 times the mass of the sun. "Stars engulfing their companions have been theorized for many decades, and this event provides the first observations of this theoretical prediction," Karambelkar said.

Sources indicate that although these findings suggest that two stars — a binary system nicknamed "Bao" — merged into one, "it is not the only possibility," Karambelkar said. "The other possibility is that both stars survived, in a much shorter orbit. In order to conclusively determine what happened, we need to continue monitoring what the system does, once the heft of the eruption settles down.".

Now that astronomers may have found the first such merger, "I can't wait to find more," Karambelkar stated. "Upcoming telescopes like the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope and the Vera Rubin Observatory will be very useful in discovering many more such events.".

Sources indicate that the scientists detailed their findings Nov. 18 in the journal Nature.

Breaking: A little-known protein could be a powerful weapon against Alzheimer’s

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1414 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, A protein that helps protect the brain may offer scientists a promising new way to fight Alzheimer's disease and other forms of dementia.
  • The findings, published in Science Advances by scientists at Sanford Burnham Prebys, suggest that strengthening the brain's own protective mechanisms could eventually lead to new treatments for neurodegenerative diseases.
  • The discovery is particularly significant because tau plays an essential role in keeping healthy brain cells functioning.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, A protein that helps protect the brain may offer scientists a promising new way to fight Alzheimer's disease and other forms of dementia. Researchers have discovered that increasing levels of this protein can reduce the buildup of toxic tangles associated with brain damage, while also helping preserve the connections that allow nerve cells to communicate.

The findings, published in Science Advances by scientists at Sanford Burnham Prebys, suggest that strengthening the brain's own protective mechanisms could eventually lead to new treatments for neurodegenerative diseases. In experiments with mice, the researchers found that boosting the protein reduced several damaging changes associated with Alzheimer's, including brain shrinkage and the accumulation of abnormal tau proteins.

The discovery is particularly significant because tau plays an essential role in keeping healthy brain cells functioning. Under normal conditions, tau proteins help stabilize microtubules, tiny structures that provide internal support to neurons and help maintain the intricate networks of the nervous system.

In Alzheimer's and several related disorders, however, tau proteins can become abnormal and stick together, forming harmful clumps known as tau tangles. These tangles disrupt the normal functioning of nerve cells and are associated with cognitive decline and neuronal death. Diseases characterized by abnormal tau accumulation are collectively called tauopathies.

A Protective Protein With a Surprising Role in Alzheimer's.

The researchers investigated a protein called sorting-related receptor with A-type repeats (SORLA), which has already attracted scientific attention for its potential role in protecting the brain against Alzheimer's disease.

It has been revealed that previous studies have shown that SORLA can help limit the production and accumulation of amyloid-beta, another protein closely associated with Alzheimer's. Amyloid-beta can build up into plaques in the brain, making it one of the disease's major pathological hallmarks alongside tau tangles.

"In the last 15 or 20 years, considerable data has come out from our lab and other groups showing that SORLA can suppress one of the hallmarks of Alzheimer's disease -- amyloid-beta generation and accumulation," remarked Timothy Huang, PhD, assistant professor in the Center for Neurologic Diseases at Sanford Burnham Prebys.

"Very little was known, however, about whether SORLA affected the tau tangles reflected on the other side of the coin in Alzheimer's disease.".

To investigate this question, the scientists developed a mouse model by breeding animals engineered to produce additional human SORLA with mice that develop tau tangles, brain atrophy, and cognitive impairments. This allowed them to examine whether higher SORLA levels could reduce tau accumulation and protect against the damage it causes.

Boosting SORLA Reduces Toxic Tau and Brain Shrinkage.

The results revealed that additional SORLA provided protection against several processes that contribute to tau tangles and the progression of neurodegenerative disease.

Sources indicate that one vital effect involved a process called hyperphosphorylation. This occurs when too many phosphate groups attach to tau proteins, altering their behavior and contributing to the development of harmful tangles. Higher SORLA levels reduced this abnormal modification.

The protein also limited the ability of misfolded tau to act as "seeds" that encourage other tau proteins to clump together. This seeding process can help toxic tau aggregates multiply and spread their damaging effects.

Industry observers note that beyond reducing tau abnormalities, SORLA helped preserve synapses, the specialized connections through which neurons communicate. It also protected synaptic plasticity, the brain's ability to strengthen or modify those connections, which is essential for learning, memory, and normal cognitive function.

"When you upregulate SORLA, you can suppress the negative effects found in tauopathies," remarked Huijie Huang, PhD, a staff scientist in the Huang lab at Sanford Burnham Prebys and lead author of the study.

"We found there was less brain atrophy and less tau accumulation, which was very exciting to see.".

Removing the Protein Makes Brain Damage Worse.

After observing the benefits of increasing SORLA, the researchers examined what would happen if the protein were missing entirely.

Recent findings suggest that SORLA is produced using instructions encoded by a gene called Sorl1. Some people carry mutations that interfere with this gene's function, potentially disrupting the production or activity of the protective protein.

To investigate the consequences, the team studied genetically modified mice that lacked Sorl1 and therefore could not produce SORLA.

Industry observers note that the results contrasted sharply with those seen in mice carrying additional copies of the protein. Instead of protecting against tau-related damage, the absence of SORLA made the harmful effects more severe.

"The opposite turned out to be true when we deleted the ability to produce SORLA proteins," noted Tim Huang, senior and corresponding author of the manuscript. "A lack of SORLA exacerbated the harmful effects observed in tauopathies.".

These contrasting results provided further evidence that SORLA plays an important protective role in the brain and may influence how severely tau-related diseases progress.

A Fresh Clue Could Lead to Alzheimer's Treatments.

To understand why changing SORLA levels had such different effects, the researchers examined the molecular activity of individual brain cells and the surrounding tissue.

They combined advanced sequencing methods to measure protein levels and gene activity in individual cells with techniques that map where RNA and proteins are located within brain tissue. This detailed approach helped reveal how SORLA influences the biological processes involved in neurodegeneration.

The analysis indicated that increasing SORLA helped prevent harmful changes in protein production at synapses while also suppressing other mechanisms associated with tauopathy progression.

Sources indicate that the researchers also discovered that higher SORLA levels reduced abnormal gene activity in glial cells. These cells perform several essential functions in the nervous system, including supporting, maintaining, and protecting neurons. Changes in glial cell activity can contribute to the progression of neurodegenerative diseases.

One finding was especially intriguing because it pointed toward a potential target for existing medications.

"One particularly notable finding that we can build on is the upregulation of a member of the plexin-B family of receptors in the absence of SORLA," remarked Huijie Huang.

Recent findings suggest that plexin-B receptors are proteins involved in cellular signaling, helping cells respond to information from their surroundings. The increased activity of a receptor in this family when SORLA was absent suggests that this signaling pathway could be involved in some of the damaging changes associated with tau disorders.

Importantly, drugs capable of targeting this family of receptors already exist, raising the possibility that scientists could investigate whether they might be useful against tau-related dementia.

"There are unique drugs that can target this class of receptors that we may be able to apply to tau-related dementia disorders," said Tim Huang. "One potential future direction is to repurpose these drugs to target overactivation of glial cells and perhaps reverse some of the phenotypes in tauopathies.".

The Next Step Toward Human Alzheimer's Research.

Although the findings are encouraging, the protective effects were demonstrated in mice, and more research is needed to determine how these mechanisms operate in humans.

Recent findings suggest that the team now hopes to investigate how individual types of brain cells respond when SORLA levels increase or decrease. One planned approach involves transplanting human neurons or glial cells into mouse brains, allowing researchers to examine the effects of different SORLA mutations in a living brain affected by disease.

"Mouse cells and human cells are different," mentioned Tim Huang. "Because we're looking at human disease, it's more informative if we can observe the modulation and dysfunction of SORLA in the context of a human cell inside of a diseased brain environment.".

These experiments could help clarify how SORLA protects neurons from toxic tau accumulation and why disruptions in its function make neurodegeneration worse.

Ultimately, the researchers hope that a deeper understanding of this protective protein will reveal newly introduced treatment strategies, either by enhancing SORLA's activity or by repurposing existing drugs to interfere with damaging cellular pathways. Such approaches could eventually offer new ways to combat Alzheimer's disease and other forms of dementia driven by toxic tau tangles.

The study was supported by the National Institutes of Health, National Cancer Institute and National Institute on Aging.
